title: Minimal Mathlib Imports for Elementary Proof
content: The proof uses only Nat.Prime, Nat.factorial, ZMod, and Tactic — a remarkably small import footprint for a theorem about prime distributions. No analytic number theory (complex analysis, L-functions, sieve methods) is needed.
mathContext: Nat.exists_prime_and_dvd: $\forall n \geq 2, \exists p$ prime with $p \mid n$. Nat.dvd_factorial: $p$ prime, $p \leq n \Rightarrow p \mid n!$. These two elementary facts are the only number-theoretic tools beyond basic arithmetic.
significance: The small import set underscores the elementary nature of this Dirichlet-class result. The primes ≡ 2 (mod 3) case is one of a handful where Euclid's method (applied with a twist for residue classes) succeeds without analytic machinery.

title: Multiplicativity of Residue 1 (mod 3)
content: mul_mod_three_one: the product of two integers ≡ 1 (mod 3) is ≡ 1 (mod 3). Proved directly from Nat.mul_mod and computation. This is the group property of (ℤ/3ℤ)* — the multiplicative group of a field — applied to the identity element 1.
mathContext: $(a \cdot b) \bmod 3 = ((a \bmod 3) \cdot (b \bmod 3)) \bmod 3 = (1 \cdot 1) \bmod 3 = 1$. More generally, the product of elements in any congruence class modulo a prime is determined by the classes. Here $(\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z})^* = \{1, 2\}$ is isomorphic to $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$.
significance: This lemma is the closure property needed for the factoring argument: if all prime factors are ≡ 1 (mod 3), the product is ≡ 1 (mod 3) by induction using this lemma. Without it, the strong induction in factors_determine_mod_three would need to unfold the full multiplicative structure.

title: factors_determine_mod_three: Strong Induction on Composite Structure
content: The key lemma: if all prime factors of n are either 3 or ≡ 1 (mod 3), then n ≢ 2 (mod 3). Proved by strong induction. The base cases handle n = 1 and prime n. The inductive step extracts a factor p ≡ 1 (mod 3), divides n = p·m, uses mul_mod to show m ≡ 2 (mod 3) if n ≡ 2 (mod 3) and p ≡ 1 (mod 3), then applies the inductive hypothesis to m < n.
mathContext: Induction: $n = p \cdot m$ with $p$ prime, $p \mid n$, $m < n$. If $p \equiv 1 \pmod{3}$, then $n \equiv p \cdot m \equiv m \pmod{3}$, so $m \equiv 2 \pmod{3}$ and we recurse to $m$. The strong induction (on $n$) terminates since $m = n/p < n$ for $p \geq 2$.
significance: This is the most technically involved lemma in the file. The use of strong induction (not simple induction) is essential: when n is composite n = p·m, we apply the inductive hypothesis to m < n. This requires knowing the result holds for ALL smaller values, not just the predecessor.

title: The Euclid-Style Construction N = 3·(n+1)! - 1
content: Given any n, construct N = 3·(n+1)! - 1. Then: (1) N ≡ 2 (mod 3) since 3 | 3·(n+1)!, so N ≡ -1 ≡ 2 (mod 3). (2) N has a prime factor p ≡ 2 (mod 3) by factors_determine_mod_three. (3) p > n: if p ≤ n+1, then p | (n+1)! (by Nat.dvd_factorial), so p | 3·(n+1)!, but also p | N, giving p | 1, contradiction. Therefore p > n is a prime ≡ 2 (mod 3) larger than n.
mathContext: $N = 3 \cdot (n+1)! - 1 \equiv -1 \equiv 2 \pmod{3}$. Size argument: $p \leq n+1 \Rightarrow p \mid (n+1)! \Rightarrow p \mid 3(n+1)! \Rightarrow p \mid (3(n+1)! - N) = 1$, contradicting $p$ prime. So $p > n+1 > n$.
significance: The N = d·M - 1 trick (here d = 3) works for any d and produces N ≡ -1 ≡ d-1 (mod d). When d-1 is a residue that forces a specific prime factor (like 2 mod 3), this gives an elementary Dirichlet-type proof. The key insight is that -1 mod d is always a 'hard' residue — it can't be achieved by products of 1-residues alone.
